hints: Start by picturing the two bodies side by side - a fungal mycelium made of hyphae, and a maize leaf made of plant cells. What wall material and what green organelle would you expect in only one of them?
Now think about food. One organism makes its own food using light, the other must take food from the maize leaves it damages. Which terms describe those two ways of life?
walkthrough:
Build the structural contrast**
Fungi and plants are both eukaryotes but their cells are built differently. Fungal walls are made of chitin, not cellulose, and fungal cells have no chloroplasts. The mycelium is a network of long branching hyphae, often multinucleate, very different from organised plant cells with cellulose walls, chloroplasts and usually one nucleus.

Link structure to nutrition**
Because it lacks chloroplasts, E. turcicum cannot photosynthesise. It lives as a heterotroph and a parasite, secreting enzymes and absorbing nutrients from the maize leaf. Z. mays has chloroplasts with chlorophyll, so it is an autotroph that photosynthesises to make its own organic food.

Final answer: Structural: E. turcicum has chitin cell walls / no chloroplasts / long branching hyphae with several nuclei per cell; Z. mays has cellulose cell walls / chloroplasts / cells with one nucleus per cell. Functional: E. turcicum is heterotrophic / parasitic, obtains food from host, does not photosynthesise; Z. mays is autotrophic / photosynthetic.

hints: Picture classification as a set of nested boxes, with the biggest box at the top. What happens to the number of organisms and the similarity between them as you go down?
Think about why organisms are put in the same box - what must they share?
Recall the order of the main ranks from large to small. Which three come after kingdom, and what is the final two-part name made of?
Both these organisms have membrane-bound nuclei, so which domain do they share, and why must they then split into two different kingdoms?
walkthrough:
Nested groups based on similarity**
Classification groups organisms by shared structural, biochemical and genetic features. You start with a very large group and split it into smaller and smaller groups. Members of a smaller group are more similar to each other than members of the larger group they came from.

Learn the rank order**
The sequence is domain - kingdom - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species. You need kingdom to family for this point. The last two ranks, genus and species, together form the binomial or Linnaean Latin scientific name, such as Exserohilum turcicum and Zea mays.

Place these two organisms**
Both have true nuclei and membrane-bound organelles, so both belong in domain Eukarya. They then diverge: E. turcicum has chitin walls and heterotrophic nutrition so belongs in kingdom Fungi, while Z. mays has cellulose walls, chloroplasts and photosynthesis so belongs in kingdom Plantae.

Final answer: Large groups are divided into smaller groups; organisms within a group share common features. Hierarchy: kingdom - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species; genus + species gives binomial scientific name. Both in domain Eukarya; in different kingdoms, Fungi and Plantae.

hints: Think about what the x-axis really means for the plant. If a leaf has only a small damaged area, has the fungus succeeded or failed?
Now read the positions of the two arrows on the x-axis. Estimate the mean % damage for SKV50 on the left and CML153 on the right and link low damage to high resistance.
walkthrough:
Interpret damage as resistance**
Percentage area of leaf damage is an inverse measure. More damage means the fungus grew well and the plant resisted poorly. Less damage means the plant limited fungal growth, so resistance is high.

Compare the parental means**
The arrows mark the parental means on Fig. 2.1. SKV50 is at about $22\%$ damage on the far left, CML153 is at about $58\%$ on the far right. Because $22 < 58$, SKV50 suffered much less damage and therefore shows the greatest resistance to E. turcicum.
Final answer: Low percentage leaf damage means high resistance to infection. Mean for SKV50 is 22% and for CML153 is 58%, so SKV50 shows greater resistance.

hints: Look at the shape in Fig. 2.1 - the bars grade smoothly from about 20% to 60% with no distinct classes and follow a bell-shaped curve. Which type of variation shows a full range of intermediates?
walkthrough:
Recognise the bell curve**
The F2 plants show every intermediate value of leaf damage between the parents, forming a smooth normal distribution curve. There are no clear-cut categories, only a continuous range. That is the hallmark of continuous variation, which is also strongly influenced by environment.

hints: Recall that the bell curve you named in (ii) is typical when a trait is not controlled by a single gene with two alleles. How many genes are usually involved?
Think about whether those genes act on different traits or all converge on the same measured trait, here percentage leaf damage or resistance.
Consider the size of effect of swapping one allele at one of those genes - would it switch the plant from resistant to susceptible, or just nudge the percentage a little?
Put those small nudges together - what word describes how the effects of different genes sum to give the final phenotype?
walkthrough:
Many genes, one trait**
This is polygenic inheritance, also called quantitative inheritance. Instead of one gene, many different genes all influence the same trait, here the percentage area of leaf damage or level of resistance.

Small and additive effects**
At each gene, different alleles have only a small effect on the phenotype. No single allele makes a plant fully resistant or fully susceptible. The final phenotype comes from adding together the effects of all the alleles present across all the genes.

Why this gives a normal curve**
In the F2, meiosis and fertilisation reshuffle these alleles into many new combinations. Some plants inherit mostly resistance alleles and cluster near the SKV50 end, some inherit mostly susceptibility alleles near the CML153 end, and most inherit a mixture and cluster in the middle around $40\%$. That segregation of many small additive effects produces continuous variation.

Final answer: Resistance / leaf damage is controlled by many / several genes; all affect the same trait; alleles of each gene have a small effect; effects are additive / combined to give the phenotype, e.g. more resistance alleles gives lower % damage.
